name: The Sun (Sol)
summary: The gravitational center of our planetary system, fusing 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium every second in its core.

name: Mercury
summary: The smallest planet and closest to the Sun, with a heavily cratered silicate crust and Caloris impact basin experiencing swings between 430°C and -180°C.

name: Venus
summary: A runaway greenhouse furnace veiled by super-rotating sulfuric acid cloud chevrons and a crushing carbon dioxide atmosphere.

name: Earth
summary: The cradle of human civilization, featuring liquid water oceans, dynamic atmospheric cloud bands, and carbon-based life.

name: The Moon (Luna)
summary: Earth's tidally locked natural satellite, scarred by dark basaltic lunar maria (Mare Imbrium, Oceanus Procellarum) and ancient anorthositic highland ray craters.

name: Mars
summary: The iron oxide-rich Red Planet, home to Olympus Mons, the Valles Marineris canyon system, dark Syrtis Major basaltic plains, and polar ice caps.

name: 1 Ceres
summary: The largest body in the main asteroid belt, containing a third of its total mass and harboring bright sodium carbonate evaporite deposits in Occator Crater.

name: Jupiter
summary: A monumental gas giant banded by turbulent ammonia cloud belts, the Great Red Spot anticyclone, and 95 moons.

name: Saturn
summary: Famous for its golden ammonia haze bands, north polar hexagon jet stream, and expansive icy ring system.

name: Uranus
summary: An ice giant knocked onto its side with an axial tilt of 97.8 degrees, veiled in a cyan methane-rich atmosphere and faint vertical rings.

name: Neptune
summary: The most distant major planet, featuring deep azure methane bands, bright high-altitude cirrus streaks, and supersonic 2,100 km/h winds.

name: 1I/'Oumuamua
summary: The first confirmed interstellar object detected visiting from beyond Sol, following an unbound hyperbolic trajectory with a cosmic-ray-reddened tholin crust.

name: 1P/Halley (Halley's Comet)
summary: The premier short-period comet, returning every 75–76 years along a highly inclined, retrograde Keplerian ellipse.

name: 90377 Sedna
summary: An extremely distant minor planet coated in crimson methane and nitrogen tholin ices. Its 11,400-year orbit swings from ~76 AU at perihelion out past 900 AU, hinting at an unobserved outer perturber.

name: Alpha Centauri
summary: Our closest stellar neighbors, composed of solar-type binary pair Rigil Kentaurus (G2V) and Toliman (K1V), orbited by red dwarf flare star Proxima Centauri.

name: Barnard's Star
summary: A high-velocity low-mass red dwarf displaying the largest known proper motion of any star relative to Sol.

name: Sirius (The Dog Star)
summary: The brightest apparent star in Earth's sky, dancing with degenerate carbon-oxygen white dwarf companion Sirius B (The Pup).

name: TRAPPIST-1
summary: A compact ultra-cool red dwarf hosting seven temperate terrestrial exoplanets, three orbiting inside the liquid-water habitable zone.

name: Polaris (North Star)
summary: Earth's north celestial pole star, a luminous yellow supergiant pulsating radially as a classic Cepheid standard candle.

name: Betelgeuse (Alpha Orionis)
summary: A semiregular pulsating red supergiant boiling with giant convection cells near core collapse, destined to end in a Type II supernova.

name: Crab Nebula & Pulsar (M1)
summary: The expanding filamentary wreckage of supernova SN 1054, powered by a central synchrotron neutron star spinning 30 times a second.

name: Orion Nebula (M42)
summary: A massive H II stellar nursery visible to the naked eye, actively birthing protoplanetary disks inside the glowing Trapezium cluster.

name: Eagle Nebula (M16 / Pillars of Creation)
type: Active Emission Nebula / H II Region
summary: A prolific stellar nursery housing the towering 'Pillars of Creation', where ultraviolet radiation from young O-type stars sculpts cold molecular gas.

name: Stephenson 2-18
summary: One of the largest known stars in the universe, an extreme red hypergiant with an estimated radius of 2,150 solar radii—large enough to engulf Saturn's orbit.

name: Sagittarius A*
summary: The 4.15-million solar-mass gravitational anchor at the nucleus of the Milky Way, surrounded by relativistic Doppler-boosted accretion flares.

name: Large Magellanic Cloud
summary: The most massive satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, featuring an off-center stellar bar and the glowing Tarantula Nebula starburst complex.

name: Small Magellanic Cloud
summary: A gas-rich dwarf irregular galaxy bound to the Milky Way, tidally stretched by past gravitational encounters with the LMC.

name: Andromeda Galaxy (M31)
summary: The largest galaxy in the Local Group, heading toward the Milky Way on a blueshifted collision trajectory at 110 km/s.

name: Triangulum Galaxy (M33)
summary: The third-largest member of the Local Group, displaying loosely wound spiral arms and prominent H II star-forming regions.

name: Sombrero Galaxy (M104)
summary: A magnificent lenticular galaxy distinguished by an extraordinarily luminous central bulge and a sharp, dark equatorial dust absorption lane.

name: Centaurus A (NGC 5128)
summary: A giant peculiar elliptical galaxy bisected by a warped dark dust lane, launching relativistic synchrotron plasma jets from its central black hole.

name: Messier 87 (Virgo A / M87*)
summary: The dominant supergiant elliptical galaxy of the Virgo Cluster, hosting a 6.5-billion-solar-mass black hole launching a 5,000-light-year relativistic jet.

name: The Great Attractor
summary: A massive gravitational focal point in the Zone of Avoidance drawing the Milky Way and hundreds of thousands of galaxies along the Laniakea Supercluster.

name: Boötes Void (The Great Nothing)
summary: A gargantuan spherical cosmic desert spanning 330 million light-years across, containing only ~60 galaxies where 2,000 would normally form.

name: Shapley Supercluster
summary: The largest concentration of gravitationally bound galaxies in the nearby universe, pulling the Laniakea Supercluster and Great Attractor toward its core.

name: El Gordo (ACT-CL J0102-4915)
summary: The most massive colliding galaxy cluster observed in the distant universe, glowing with shock-heated X-ray intracluster plasma across 3 quadrillion solar masses.

name: SMACS J0723.3-7327
summary: A massive galaxy cluster bending spacetime into an Einstein gravitational lens, famous as the target of JWST's First Deep Field.

name: TON 618
summary: The largest known ultramassive black hole (66 billion solar masses), featuring a 390-billion-kilometer (~2,600 AU) event horizon that dwarfs our entire Solar System, a relativistic quasar jet, and a golden-orange accretion disk shining with the power of 140 trillion Suns.

name: Earendel (WHL0137-LS)
summary: The most distant individual star ever detected, observed 900 million years after the Big Bang via gravitational lensing magnification.

name: GN-z11
summary: An intensely star-forming primordial galaxy observed just 400 million years after the Big Bang, strongly redshifted into the infrared.
